Situation1: They greet a few customers politely while scanning items at a quiet store.
Expectation2: Raise public awareness about social inequities and marginalized groups
Situation2: They respond to an urgent incident of discrimination that requires immediate public attention and awareness.
Story: I stood behind the register, the soft beep of scanned groceries filling the quiet store. I smiled at Mrs. Lee, who always chatted about her grandkids, and nodded politely to the young man behind her. As a cashier, I knew the importance of making every customer feel welcome, of keeping the line moving smoothly, of being the friendly face people expected. But as I handed Mrs. Lee her receipt, my phone buzzed in my pocket—a message from the advocacy group I worked with. There’d been an incident of discrimination at a nearby business, and they needed someone to respond, to post on social media, to rally support and raise awareness immediately. My heart pounded. I could picture the faces of those affected, waiting for someone to speak up. But here, at the register, customers expected my full attention, my patience, my smile. I felt torn, the weight of both roles pressing on me, each demanding something I wasn’t sure I could give at the same time.
